title: Live Hosted Gen Orientation: streams, params & failure modes
summary: Introductory hosted API demo focusing on chat/generation basics: streaming behavior, key parameters, retry/backoff strategies, and failure-mode handling. Customer is evaluating Redwood for a patient-facing conversational assistant and has strict latency and data residency concerns. Key asks: SOC2 + audit logs, VPC/private deployment options, and a short pilot with throughput targets. Agreed to share security pack and a trial sandbox repo.
action_items: Alex Kim - send SOC2 + security pack and private deployment one-pager (2027-06-04)
Priya Das - provide sample benchmark script and recommended params for 99th percentile <350ms target (2027-06-07)
Jordan Lee - provide expected qps and 95/99 latency targets, and list of PII flows (2027-06-06)
next_steps: Send security docs + dedicated vs hosted comparison
Provision read-only sandbox org and share credentials
Schedule pilot kick-off next week (30-45 min)
Run small benchmark with customer dataset and share results
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02 15:30 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Das (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO - Cobalt), Maya Rivera (Lead Eng), Samir Patel (SRE), Ellen Brooks (PM)
Links shared: deck: https://redwood.ai/deck/hosted-gen-intro (short link), security pack note: /docs/soc2-summ.pdf, benchmark sheet: https://sheets.example/bench-cobalt

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. Quick intro, Priya will do a live run through of the hosted API and show streaming plus some parameter knobs and failure handling.
00:18 Jordan: Great thanks, small ask up front — we have a latency SLO around 200ms p95 for single-turn prompts in production, is that realistic with hosted?
00:30 Priya: Quick answer, usually p95 at 200 is ambitious depending on model size and prompt length but we can get close with the right model selection and aggressive batching/caching disabled for low-latency paths. For hosted we have variants optimized for low latency.
00:47 Maya: When you say "variants" do you mean smaller quantized models or different kernel configs?
00:52 Priya: Both — model variants can be quantized or compiled with different kernel selections. We also have the option to run on Dedicated capacity if you need strict throughput guarantees. Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs, predictable latency.
01:08 Ellen: For compliance, is hosted allowed for PHI? We are a health company so that matters.
01:16 Alex: Short: hosted can be used but many healthcare customers prefer Private (VPC) or on-prem for PHI. We'll send the SOC2 + KMS/HSM notes. You also asked about audit logs — those are part of the Console (per-token traces, request metadata).
01:34 Samir: Quick technical: how does streaming work on your API? Is it server-sent events? Websocket?
01:42 Priya: We support chunked HTTP streaming and also websockets for long-lived sessions. The streaming is incremental: tokens arrive as they're generated. If you need deterministic latency we recommend tuning max_new_tokens and response_length and enabling early-stopping rules.
02:05 Alex: Let's jump into a quick demo. Priya, take it away.
02:10 Priya: Ok sharing screen — I'll run a quick curl sample to show streaming then show how retries look if a 500 happens.
02:22 Priya: (typing) Here is a simple chat call: role: user with a short system prompt and a small message. Params: model: redwood-2s-small, max_tokens: 64, temperature: 0.2, stream: true.
02:40 System noise / typing
03:00 Priya: You can see tokens begin streaming immediately; latency between first token and request is ~70ms in this region since we're using the low-latency variant.
03:18 Jordan: Is that with or without prefix caching?
03:22 Priya: Without — caching can help for repeated prefixes but adds jitter; for lowest deterministic latency we don't rely on caching.
03:30 Maya: For our assistant, many prompts are short so small model seems fine cost-wise. But we also need longer context for follow-ups. How does KV cache affect the streaming?
03:44 Priya: For multi-turns we keep KV cache warm. Streaming works the same but the generation per-turn benefits from cache warmness — which reduces per-token compute. However cache hits are best for repeated contexts; uncommon user inputs don't see much lift.
04:05 Priya: Now I'll purposely simulate an intermittent 502 to show retry behavior. (switch) We recommend idempotency keys for non-streaming calls. For streaming we use resume tokens and ephemeral session ids. If the connection drops, client can reconnect and request from last-seen token index.
04:34 Samir: So you don't re-generate the entire response on reconnect?
04:38 Priya: Correct, resume logic fetches the last kv-offset and continues if the backend still has session state. We have a short TTL for session state (configurable).
04:52 Ellen: If we want guaranteed consistency, what's the recommended approach?
04:56 Priya: For critical flows, do server-side deterministic prompts + idempotency for final-output writes, and send shorter streaming chunks to reduce re-gen window. Also persist conversational state in your DB and reconcile final tokens on success.
05:15 Jordan: On retries backoff strategy, do you have a built-in client SDK or should we implement exponential backoff ourselves?
05:22 Alex: We ship SDKs that include default retry/backoff policies; you can override. The Console also surfaces retry rates per-route.
05:31 Maya: What about rate limiting? We have spikes during morning ET triage.
05:36 Priya: Hosted offers per-key rate limits and burst windows; Dedicated gives more generous burst capacity and autoscaling options. We can set spike protection with queue depth limits and graceful fallback to a smaller model.
05:55 Jordan: That fallback idea—can you route to cheaper model automatically?
05:59 Priya: Yes, Smart routing rules can downgrade to a compatible fallback model based on latency or cost policies. You define acceptable quality deltas.
06:10 Jordan: Nice. For the pilot, we expect 150 qps sustained with 1k concurrent users. Any concerns?
06:18 Priya: For hosted, sustained 150 qps depends on model choice; it's feasible but we'd typically recommend Dedicated if you need steady high qps plus strict p95 SLAs. We can propose a pilot mix: hosted sandbox followed by Dedicated commitment if numbers look stable.
06:33 Alex: I'll capture that as a success criteria: 150 qps with average latency <200ms and p95 under 350ms.
06:40 Ellen: About data residency — do you host EU/US separately? We have EU patients so must keep data in-region.
06:46 Alex: Yes, we have region selection and Private deployments that let you stay in a VPC in your chosen region. We'll include region cert details in the security pack.
06:56 Priya: Back to parameters — quick knobs: temperature for creativity, top_p for nucleus, max_tokens to bound cost, presence/ frequency penalties to modulate repetitiveness. For chat we also recommend system messages and stop sequences for deterministic truncation.
07:18 Maya: Any gotchas with stop sequences and streaming?
07:22 Priya: If you rely on stop tokens, stream may still send the final token then close. Client should enforce final trimming. Sometimes ASR/transcription services treat punctuation oddly, so be conservative with stop tokens that include punctuation.
07:41 Jordan: How about token accounting and billing? We need clear unit economics for CFO.
07:46 Alex: Billing is per-token for generations and per-embedding for embeddings. Console breakdown shows token counts per request, costs, and even route-level spend. We'll provide a sample cost calculator.
08:02 Priya: Ok quick pause — any other compliance questions?
08:06 Samir: SSO? SCIM? We'll need SAML SSO, RBAC and org-level role mapping.
08:12 Alex: Yes SAML/SSO + SCIM provisioning supported for Private and Dedicated; hosted supports SSO for enterprise accounts. RBAC and audit logs are standard.
08:25 Maya: For encryption-in-transit and at-rest, do you support customer-managed keys?
08:30 Alex: We support KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated; hosted supports platform-managed keys but we can enable CMEK for dedicated customers.
08:40 Priya: Now I'll demonstrate parameter tuning — show variance in responses for temp 0.2 vs 0.8 and how streaming speed and token counts change.
09:00 Priya: Example A low temp: reply more deterministic, fewer tokens typically. Example B high temp: more varied. Watch for length differences which affect latency and cost.
09:22 Priya: I'm also going to show console where you can pin model versions, create rollout policies and check per-route latency charts. (switch) Here is a chart showing 95th percentile over time and per-model comparison.
09:45 Ellen: If we pin to a version and you roll out a backend kernel change, do we get auto-updates?
09:50 Priya: We won't change pinned model versions without notice; rollouts are explicit and you can do canary A/B from the Console.
10:03 Jordan: For pilot success, we want a 2-week proof with production-like traffic. Can Redwood run the benchmark or do we run it?
10:12 Alex: We can help run an initial benchmark — Priya will supply the script and recommended parameters, you can run in sandbox and we run a server-side benchmark as well to cross-validate.
10:22 Priya: I'll attach the script and include warm-up sequences, concurrency ramps and a sample dataset scrubbed for PHI so we avoid leaking.
10:30 Samir: About session TTLs you mentioned earlier — what is default?
10:34 Priya: Default is 30 minutes for ephemeral session state; adjustable on Dedicated/Private.
10:40 Maya: Any limits on context window? We need 16k for long medical histories.
10:44 Priya: We support up to 32k on some variants; cost and latency increase with length. We recommend chunking and retrieval-augmented generation for extremely long histories.
10:56 Jordan: Talking about RAG — does Redwood provide vector DB or do we integrate with existing ones?
11:02 Priya: We integrate with common vector DBs; Console has connectors and embedding endpoints for ingestion. We don't host a managed vector DB in Hosted by default, but can recommend partners.
11:14 Ellen: Any known limitations or common failure modes we should watch for in production?
11:20 Priya: Network flaps on client side, long tail token bursts (very long outputs), and model OOM on oversized batch sizes. Best practices: cap max_tokens, set per-request timeouts, use idempotency for writes, and use fallbacks.
11:36 Alex: Quick note about fallbacks — we can auto-route to a lower-cost model or return cached answer if quality delta is acceptable. This reduces user-perceived failure.
11:48 Priya: I'll simulate a reconnect flow now — dropping the connection and resuming with a resume token. (demo) On client reconnect we use the session id + last token index, server sends remaining tokens.
12:10 Jordan: That sounds useful. If session state TTL config affects resumes, what is the worst-case? If TTL expires mid-session does the API return an error we can handle gracefully?
12:20 Priya: If TTL expired, you get a session-missing response and would need to regen the last turn; we return clear error codes so clients can fall back to a shorter prompt or show transient error to user.
12:36 Maya: Let's talk cost controls — can we cap spend per-user or per-route?
12:41 Alex: Console lets you set per-route quotas, token caps, and alerts. For enterprise we can set hard caps and webhook triggers.
12:52 Ellen: Timeline question — if we decide to pilot next week, how fast can we get a sandbox provisioned?
12:57 Alex: Usually 24-48 hours for a read-only sandbox. For Dedicated trial it's longer — a few days to set up reserved capacity.
13:06 Alex: Final recap — action items and deliverables?
13:10 Alex: We'll send security pack and region info, Priya will share the benchmark script and recommended params, customer will share expected traffic profile and PII flows. We'll schedule pilot kick-off.
13:22 Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks Alex and Priya, this was helpful.
13:26 Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by Friday with docs and sandbox creds.
13:30 End meeting.
